subject: Simple model yielding strange estimates and failing to converge

messages.author: 3ab4a021861e22ff
messages.subject: Simple model yielding strange estimates and failing to converge
parts:
Hi all,

I am trying to fit a very simple linear regression model that propogates estimation uncertainty in the dependant variable (it's a log-log univariate model). This is for the purposes of a simulation, but I have used several variations of this model previously for real datasets - it has always yielded the expected/logical coefficient estimates, and has converged fine. The relationship I am simulating is invariably positive (although in empirical datasets it could be negative, so I don't want to constrain the priors to positive values). However, I am repeatedly getting unfeasible negative slope estimates, alongside very large Rhat values and small (or 0) n.effs. 

Wierdly, the model itself (and variations, including multivariate models and models with alternative link functions) are still performing perfectly fine on my previously analysed, empirical data. 

I attach here a reproducible, simplified version of my simulation process, plus the model itself. I feel like there is probably a very obvious fix, but all my trials with various priors, numbers of iterations, and model formulations have led me nowhere. 

Thanks very much for any help,

Ciar

install.packages('pacman')
library(pacman)
p_load(nimble, betafunctions, MCMCvis, metafor)

#Generate masses corresponding to each sample
n_samples <- 25
min_mass <- 10
max_mass <- 20000

masses <- ceiling(rBeta.4P(n = (n_samples-2),
                            l = min_mass, u = max_mass,  
                            alpha = 1, beta = 4))
masses <- c(min_mass, masses, max_mass)
masses <- masses[order(masses)]

#Define true model parameters
b <- 0.3
a <- 2.5
exp_Value <- exp(a + log(masses) * b)

#Simulate an estimation process for the dependent variable (point estimates +- SD)
Est_Value <- c()
Est_ValueSD <- runif(n_samples, 0.1, 2)

for(i in 1:n_samples){
  Est_Value[i] <- rnorm(1, exp_Value[i], 15)
}

plot(log(masses), log(Est_Value))


#Fit NIMBLE model
mod_data <- list(n = n_samples, mass = masses, N = Est_Value, psd = Est_ValueSD)

loglog_model <- nimbleCode({
 
  #Priors
  a ~ dnorm(0, 0.0001) #Intercept Prior
  b ~ dnorm(0, 0.0001) #slope prior
  sd.resids ~ dunif(0, 10) #SD of Residuals
  tau.resids <- pow(sd.resids, -2) #Precision of residuals
 
  #Likelihood
  for(p in 1:n){
    tau.psd[p] <- pow(psd[p], -2) #Known residual component - aka measurement error
    eps[p] ~ dnorm(0, tau.resids) #Standard residual component
    log(muN[p]) <- a + log(mass[p]) * b + eps[p] #Add residual error to model
    N[p] ~ dnorm(muN[p], tau.psd[p]) #Measurement error for estimates
  }
 
})

outs <- c('a', 'b') #Monitors
inits <- list(a = rnorm(1), b = rnorm(1)) #Initial values

#Run Model
model <- nimbleModel(loglog_model, constants = mod_data, inits = inits)
MCMCconf <- configureMCMC(model, monitors = outs)
MCMC <- buildMCMC(MCMCconf)
compModel <- compileNimble(model)
compMCMC <- compileNimble(MCMC, project = compModel)
outputs <- runMCMC(compMCMC, niter = 50000, nburnin = 10000,
                     thin = 10, nchains = 4, samplesAsCodaMCMC = T)

#Gather parameter estimates +- CIs
MCMCsummary(outputs)

#Compare to normal lm and frequentist meta-analysis
lm(log(Est_Value) ~ log(masses))
rma(log(Est_Value) ~ log(masses), sei = Est_ValueSD, method = 'FE', digits = 5)

messages.author: c9e9cbbfb3b043f0
messages.subject: Re: Simple model yielding strange estimates and failing to converge
parts:
Great question, Ciar.  I think there's a fundamental difference in how you were modelling the hierarchical (nimble) model code, versus what the call to lm() doing.  I believe a log-log linear model is truly:

log(yi) ~ N(a + b*log(xi), sigma)

That, above, I believe is the model that a call like lm(log(Est_Value) ~ log(masses)) fits.

In contrast, your nimble model code specifies the relationship:

yi ~ N(exp(a + b*log(xi)), sigma)

which is fundamentally different, in that the marginal distribution of the data is normal in one case, and log-normal in the other case.

There are other minor additions in your model, specifically the "eps" terms, which I'm not addressing here.  But that said, the slightly modified hierarchical model code below gives results that well-match the results from the log-log model using lm().  Note that I've also split up your "mod_data" list into separate "mod_constants" and "mod_data" lists, which is preferable in nimble:


#Fit NIMBLE model
##mod_data <- list(n = n_samples, mass = masses, N = Est_Value, psd = Est_ValueSD)
mod_constants <- list(n = n_samples, mass = masses, psd = Est_ValueSD)
mod_data <- list(logN = log(Est_Value))

loglog_model <- nimbleCode({
    #Priors
    a ~ dnorm(0, 0.0001) #Intercept Prior
    b ~ dnorm(0, 0.0001) #slope prior
    sd.resids ~ dunif(0, 10) #SD of Residuals
    tau.resids <- pow(sd.resids, -2) #Precision of residuals
    #Likelihood
    for(p in 1:n){
        tau.psd[p] <- pow(psd[p], -2) #Known residual component - aka measurement error
        eps[p] ~ dnorm(0, tau.resids) #Standard residual component

##log(muN[p]) <- a + log(mass[p]) * b + eps[p] #Add residual error to model
        ##N[p] ~ dnorm(muN[p], tau.psd[p]) #Measurement error for estimates
        muN[p] <- a + log(mass[p]) * b + eps[p] #Add residual error to model
        logN[p] ~ dnorm(muN[p], tau.psd[p]) #Measurement error for estimates

}
})

outs <- c('a', 'b') #Monitors
inits <- list(a = rnorm(1), b = rnorm(1)) #Initial values

#Run Model

##model <- nimbleModel(loglog_model, constants = mod_data, inits = inits)
model <- nimbleModel(loglog_model, constants = mod_constants, data = mod_data, inits = inits)


Please let me know if this gets you going forward, or if you have other questions.

Cheers,
Daniel

Thanks very much Daniel, this has solved it and makes a lot of sense. I am glad to have learned something! 

I now understand that my model assumes multiplicative error (eps in my specification). In my application, allowing error to increase with the dependant variable does make sense, but I'm interested in how to specify the model with additive error. I've come up with this, which yields realistic estimates with reasonable CIs, but the Rhat values are high and N.effs low, so I am assume I have overlooked something here too:
mod_constants <- list(n = n_samples, mass = masses, psd = Est_ValueSD)
mod_data <- list(N = Est_Value)

loglog_model <- nimbleCode({
  #Priors
  a ~ dnorm(0, 0.0001) #Intercept Prior
  b ~ dnorm(0, 0.0001) #slope prior
  sd.resids ~ dunif(0, 10) #SD of Residuals
  tau.resids <- pow(sd.resids, -2) #Precision of residuals
  #Likelihood
  for(p in 1:n){
    tau.psd[p] <- pow(psd[p], -2) #Known residual component - aka measurement error
    eps[p] ~ dnorm(0, tau.resids) #Standard residual component
muN[p] <- exp(a + log(mass[p]) * b) + eps[p] #Add residual error to model

N[p] ~ dnorm(muN[p], tau.psd[p]) #Measurement error for estimates
   
  }
})

Best,

Ciar

messages.author: c9e9cbbfb3b043f0
messages.subject: Re: Simple model yielding strange estimates and failing to converge
parts:
Try centering the (log) mass covariate.  You were having near-perfect (negative) correlation between a and b in the posterior samples, see, for example:

> cor(samples)
           a          b
a  1.0000000 -0.9993901
b -0.9993901  1.0000000

Centering is a standard technique, which in this linear form will help reduce the correlation between the coefficient of the centered parameter (b), and the intercept (a).  Otherwise, while still a "valid" MCMC, the values of a and b are essentially trading off with one another, and will take prohibitively long to mix and give good estimates of the posterior distributions (as reflected by your low N.eff values).   Essentially, try this:

##mod_constants <- list(n = n_samples, mass = masses, psd = Est_ValueSD)
mod_constants <- list(n = n_samples,

logmass_centered = log(masses) - mean(log(masses)),
                      psd = Est_ValueSD)

mod_data <- list(N = Est_Value)

loglog_model <- nimbleCode({
    #Priors
    a ~ dnorm(0, 0.0001) #Intercept Prior
    b ~ dnorm(0, 0.0001) #slope prior
    sd.resids ~ dunif(0, 10) #SD of Residuals
    tau.resids <- pow(sd.resids, -2) #Precision of residuals
    #Likelihood
    for(p in 1:n){
        tau.psd[p] <- pow(psd[p], -2) #Known residual component - aka measurement error
        eps[p] ~ dnorm(0, tau.resids) #Standard residual component

##muN[p] <- exp(a + log(mass[p]) * b) + eps[p] #Add residual error to model
        muN[p] <- exp(a + logmass_centered[p] * b) + eps[p] #Add residual error to model

N[p] ~ dnorm(muN[p], tau.psd[p]) #Measurement error for estimates
    }
})

Cheers, Happy Sunday,
Daniel

exp_Value <- exp(a + log(masses) * b)

#Simulate an estimation process for the dependent variable (point estimates +- SD)
Est_Value <- c()
Est_ValueSD <- runif(n_samples, 0.1, 2)

for(i in 1:n_samples){
  Est_Value[i] <- rnorm(1, exp_Value[i], 15)
}

plot(log(masses), log(Est_Value))


#Fit NIMBLE model
mod_data <- list(n = n_samples, mass = masses, N = Est_Value, psd = Est_ValueSD)

loglog_model <- nimbleCode({
 
  #Priors
  a ~ dnorm(0, 0.0001) #Intercept Prior
  b ~ dnorm(0, 0.0001) #slope prior
  sd.resids ~ dunif(0, 10) #SD of Residuals
  tau.resids <- pow(sd.resids, -2) #Precision of residuals
 
  #Likelihood
  for(p in 1:n){
    tau.psd[p] <- pow(psd[p], -2) #Known residual component - aka measurement error
    eps[p] ~ dnorm(0, tau.resids) #Standard residual component
    log(muN[p]) <- a + log(mass[p]) * b + eps[p] #Add residual error to model
    N[p] ~ dnorm(muN[p], tau.psd[p]) #Measurement error for estimates
  }
 
})

outs <- c('a', 'b') #Monitors
inits <- list(a = rnorm(1), b = rnorm(1)) #Initial values

#Run Model
model <- nimbleModel(loglog_model, constants = mod_data, inits = inits)
MCMCconf <- configureMCMC(model, monitors = outs)
MCMC <- buildMCMC(MCMCconf)
compModel <- compileNimble(model)
compMCMC <- compileNimble(MCMC, project = compModel)
outputs <- runMCMC(compMCMC, niter = 50000, nburnin = 10000,
                     thin = 10, nchains = 4, samplesAsCodaMCMC = T)

#Gather parameter estimates +- CIs
MCMCsummary(outputs)

#Compare to normal lm and frequentist meta-analysis
lm(log(Est_Value) ~ log(masses))
rma(log(Est_Value) ~ log(masses), sei = Est_ValueSD, method = 'FE', digits = 5)

On Sunday, November 6, 2022 at 3:24:13 PM UTC db...@williams.edu wrote:
Try centering the (log) mass covariate.  You were having near-perfect (negative) correlation between a and b in the posterior samples, see, for example:

> cor(samples)
           a          b
a  1.0000000 -0.9993901
b -0.9993901  1.0000000

Centering is a standard technique, which in this linear form will help reduce the correlation between the coefficient of the centered parameter (b), and the intercept (a).  Otherwise, while still a "valid" MCMC, the values of a and b are essentially trading off with one another, and will take prohibitively long to mix and give good estimates of the posterior distributions (as reflected by your low N.eff values).   Essentially, try this:

##mod_constants <- list(n = n_samples, mass = masses, psd = Est_ValueSD)

mod_constants <- list(n = n_samples,
                      logmass_centered = log(masses) - mean(log(masses)),
                      psd = Est_ValueSD)

mod_data <- list(N = Est_Value)

loglog_model <- nimbleCode({
    #Priors
    a ~ dnorm(0, 0.0001) #Intercept Prior
    b ~ dnorm(0, 0.0001) #slope prior
    sd.resids ~ dunif(0, 10) #SD of Residuals
    tau.resids <- pow(sd.resids, -2) #Precision of residuals
    #Likelihood
    for(p in 1:n){
        tau.psd[p] <- pow(psd[p], -2) #Known residual component - aka measurement error
        eps[p] ~ dnorm(0, tau.resids) #Standard residual component
        ##muN[p] <- exp(a + log(mass[p]) * b) + eps[p] #Add residual error to model
        muN[p] <- exp(a + logmass_centered[p] * b) + eps[p] #Add residual error to model

        N[p] ~ dnorm(muN[p], tau.psd[p]) #Measurement error for estimates
    }
})


Cheers, Happy Sunday,
Daniel

On Friday, November 4, 2022 at 3:57:19 PM UTC db...@williams.edu wrote:
Great question, Ciar.  I think there's a fundamental difference in how you were modelling the hierarchical (nimble) model code, versus what the call to lm() doing.  I believe a log-log linear model is truly:

log(yi) ~ N(a + b*log(xi), sigma)

That, above, I believe is the model that a call like lm(log(Est_Value) ~ log(masses)) fits.

In contrast, your nimble model code specifies the relationship:

yi ~ N(exp(a + b*log(xi)), sigma)

which is fundamentally different, in that the marginal distribution of the data is normal in one case, and log-normal in the other case.

There are other minor additions in your model, specifically the "eps" terms, which I'm not addressing here.  But that said, the slightly modified hierarchical model code below gives results that well-match the results from the log-log model using lm().  Note that I've also split up your "mod_data" list into separate "mod_constants" and "mod_data" lists, which is preferable in nimble:


#Fit NIMBLE model
##mod_data <- list(n = n_samples, mass = masses, N = Est_Value, psd = Est_ValueSD)
mod_constants <- list(n = n_samples, mass = masses, psd = Est_ValueSD)
mod_data <- list(logN = log(Est_Value))


loglog_model <- nimbleCode({
    #Priors
    a ~ dnorm(0, 0.0001) #Intercept Prior
    b ~ dnorm(0, 0.0001) #slope prior
    sd.resids ~ dunif(0, 10) #SD of Residuals
    tau.resids <- pow(sd.resids, -2) #Precision of residuals
    #Likelihood
    for(p in 1:n){
        tau.psd[p] <- pow(psd[p], -2) #Known residual component - aka measurement error
        eps[p] ~ dnorm(0, tau.resids) #Standard residual component
        ##log(muN[p]) <- a + log(mass[p]) * b + eps[p] #Add residual error to model
        ##N[p] ~ dnorm(muN[p], tau.psd[p]) #Measurement error for estimates
        muN[p] <- a + log(mass[p]) * b + eps[p] #Add residual error to model
        logN[p] ~ dnorm(muN[p], tau.psd[p]) #Measurement error for estimates

    }
})

outs <- c('a', 'b') #Monitors
inits <- list(a = rnorm(1), b = rnorm(1)) #Initial values

#Run Model
##model <- nimbleModel(loglog_model, constants = mod_data, inits = inits)
model <- nimbleModel(loglog_model, constants = mod_constants, data = mod_data, inits = inits)


Please let me know if this gets you going forward, or if you have other questions.

Cheers,
Daniel




On Thu, Nov 3, 2022 at 12:39 PM Ciar Noble <ciar...@gmail.com> wrote:
Hi all,

I am trying to fit a very simple linear regression model that propogates estimation uncertainty in the dependant variable (it's a log-log univariate model). This is for the purposes of a simulation, but I have used several variations of this model previously for real datasets - it has always yielded the expected/logical coefficient estimates, and has converged fine. The relationship I am simulating is invariably positive (although in empirical datasets it could be negative, so I don't want to constrain the priors to positive values). However, I am repeatedly getting unfeasible negative slope estimates, alongside very large Rhat values and small (or 0) n.effs. 

Wierdly, the model itself (and variations, including multivariate models and models with alternative link functions) are still performing perfectly fine on my previously analysed, empirical data. 

I attach here a reproducible, simplified version of my simulation process, plus the model itself. I feel like there is probably a very obvious fix, but all my trials with various priors, numbers of iterations, and model formulations have led me nowhere. 

Thanks very much for any help,

Ciar

install.packages('pacman')
library(pacman)
p_load(nimble, betafunctions, MCMCvis, metafor)

#Generate masses corresponding to each sample
n_samples <- 25
min_mass <- 10
max_mass <- 20000

masses <- ceiling(rBeta.4P(n = (n_samples-2),
                            l = min_mass, u = max_mass,  
                            alpha = 1, beta = 4))
masses <- c(min_mass, masses, max_mass)
masses <- masses[order(masses)]

#Define true model parameters
b <- 0.3
a <- 2.5
exp_Value <- exp(a + log(masses) * b)

#Simulate an estimation process for the dependent variable (point estimates +- SD)
Est_Value <- c()
Est_ValueSD <- runif(n_samples, 0.1, 2)

for(i in 1:n_samples){
  Est_Value[i] <- rnorm(1, exp_Value[i], 15)
}

plot(log(masses), log(Est_Value))


#Fit NIMBLE model
mod_data <- list(n = n_samples, mass = masses, N = Est_Value, psd = Est_ValueSD)

loglog_model <- nimbleCode({
 
  #Priors
  a ~ dnorm(0, 0.0001) #Intercept Prior
  b ~ dnorm(0, 0.0001) #slope prior
  sd.resids ~ dunif(0, 10) #SD of Residuals
  tau.resids <- pow(sd.resids, -2) #Precision of residuals
 
  #Likelihood
  for(p in 1:n){
    tau.psd[p] <- pow(psd[p], -2) #Known residual component - aka measurement error
    eps[p] ~ dnorm(0, tau.resids) #Standard residual component
    log(muN[p]) <- a + log(mass[p]) * b + eps[p] #Add residual error to model
    N[p] ~ dnorm(muN[p], tau.psd[p]) #Measurement error for estimates
  }
 
})

outs <- c('a', 'b') #Monitors
inits <- list(a = rnorm(1), b = rnorm(1)) #Initial values

#Run Model
model <- nimbleModel(loglog_model, constants = mod_data, inits = inits)
MCMCconf <- configureMCMC(model, monitors = outs)
MCMC <- buildMCMC(MCMCconf)
compModel <- compileNimble(model)
compMCMC <- compileNimble(MCMC, project = compModel)
outputs <- runMCMC(compMCMC, niter = 50000, nburnin = 10000,
                     thin = 10, nchains = 4, samplesAsCodaMCMC = T)

#Gather parameter estimates +- CIs
MCMCsummary(outputs)

#Compare to normal lm and frequentist meta-analysis
lm(log(Est_Value) ~ log(masses))
rma(log(Est_Value) ~ log(masses), sei = Est_ValueSD, method = 'FE', digits = 5)
